back: A table that groups data into [[imp:classes (intervals)]] and shows the number of values ([[kw:frequency]]) in each class.
It reveals patterns in large data sets.
$$\text{Class Width} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Range}}{\text{Number of Classes}} \right\rceil$$
[[imp:Always round up.]]
$$\text{Midpoint} = \frac{\text{Lower Limit} + \text{Upper Limit}}{2}$$
Used as a representative value for the class.
cards.front: What is the [[kw:midpoint]] of a class?

back: $$\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{\text{Class Frequency } f}{\text{Sample Size } n}$$
Proportion of data in a class; sum ≈ 1.
The running total of frequencies up to and including a class.
The cumulative frequency of the last class equals [[imp:the total sample size $n$]].
A bar graph for quantitative data where consecutive bars [[imp:touch]].
Uses class boundaries on the horizontal axis, frequencies on the vertical axis.
Lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5; Upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5.
They [[imp:eliminate gaps]] between histogram bars.
cards.front: What are [[kw:class boundaries]] for integer data?

back: A line graph that plots frequency at each class [[imp:midpoint]] and connects them.
Extended to the horizontal axis before the first and after the last class.
A cumulative frequency graph (line graph).
Plots cumulative frequency at [[imp:upper class boundaries]]; always slopes upward.
Split each number into a [[imp:stem]] (leading digits) and a [[imp:leaf]] (final digit).
Preserves original values; always include a key.
Each data value is shown as a [[imp:dot]] above its value on a horizontal axis.
Stacks of dots show frequency; best for small data sets.
$$\text{Central Angle} = 360° \times \frac{\text{Category Frequency}}{n}$$
The area of each sector is proportional to its relative frequency.
cards.front: How do you compute the central angle for a [[kw:pie chart]]?

back: A vertical bar graph for qualitative data with bars arranged [[imp:from tallest to shortest]].
Highlights the most important categories.
To display the relationship between two [[imp:quantitative variables]].
Rising trend → positive association; falling trend → negative association.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:scatter plot]] used for?

back: Data collected at regular time intervals.
A time series chart plots time on the horizontal axis, connects points to show trends.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:mean]] of a data set.
back: Sum of all data values divided by the number of values.
Sample: $ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} $; Population: $ \mu = \frac{\sum x}{N} $.
Order the data; the median is the [[imp:middle value]].
Odd $n$: center entry; even $n$: average of two center entries.
Resistant to outliers.
The most frequent value(s) in the data set.
Can be unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, or none.
The only measure of center for qualitative data.
$$ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum (x \cdot w)}{\sum w} $$
Used when data values have different degrees of importance (weights).

cards.front: How do you approximate the mean from a [[kw:grouped frequency distribution]]?
back: Use class [[imp:midpoints]] $x$ and frequencies $f$.
$$ \bar{x} \approx \frac{\sum (x \cdot f)}{n} $$
The left and right halves are approximate mirror images.
Mean, median, and mode are equal in a symmetric unimodal distribution.
The [[imp:tail extends to the right]].
Typically, mean > median > mode.
Example: personal incomes.
The [[imp:tail extends to the left]].
Typically, mean < median < mode.
Example: age at death.
The mean is pulled toward the outlier; the [[imp:median is resistant]].
For skewed data or data with outliers, the median is often a better measure of center.
cards.front: How does an [[kw:outlier]] affect the mean and median?
Define the [[kw:range]] of a data set.
back: Range = Maximum – Minimum.
Simplest measure of variation; uses only two values; sensitive to outliers.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:deviation]] from the mean?
back: The difference between a data value and the mean ($x - \mu$ or $x - \bar{x}$).
The sum of all deviations is always [[imp:zero]].
Variance: $ \sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N} $.
Standard deviation: $ \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2} $.
Standard deviation has the same units as the data.

cards.front: What is the difference between $\sigma$ and $s$?
back: $\sigma$ divides by $N$ (population); $s$ divides by [[imp:$n-1$]] (sample).
$s$ is an estimator of $\sigma$; $n-1$ corrects bias.
For bell‑shaped distributions: about 68% of data within $1\sigma$, 95% within $2\sigma$, 99.7% within $3\sigma$ of the mean.
For any data set, at least $1 - 1/k^2$ of the data lie within $k$ standard deviations of the mean.
For $k=2$, at least 75%; for $k=3$, at least 88.9%.

cards.front: How do you approximate the [[kw:standard deviation for grouped data]]?
back: Use class midpoints $x$ and frequencies $f$.
$$ s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 f}{n-1}} $$
An approximation because raw data are unknown.
$Q_1$: about 25% of data below it; $Q_2$: median (50% below); $Q_3$: about 75% below.
They divide an ordered data set into four equal parts.

cards.front: How do you find the [[kw:interquartile range (IQR)]]?
back: Represents the range of the middle 50% of the data; resistant to outliers.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:1.5 × IQR rule]] for identifying outliers?
back: Lower fence = $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$; Upper fence = $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.
Any value outside the fences is an [[imp:outlier]].
Minimum, $Q_1$, Median, $Q_3$, Maximum.
Used to draw a box-and-whisker plot.
A graph based on the five‑number summary.
Box from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, line at median, whiskers to min and max.
A longer whisker indicates skewness in that direction.
The $k$th percentile is a value below which $k$% of the data fall.
Ex: $Q_1$ = 25th percentile, Median = 50th percentile, $Q_3$ = 75th percentile.

cards.front: Define a [[kw:z‑score]] and give the formula.
back: The number of standard deviations a value $x$ is from the mean.
$$ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $$
Positive: above mean; Negative: below mean; Zero: at mean.

cards.front: What z‑scores are considered unusual in a bell‑shaped distribution?
back: Values with $z < -2$ or $z > 2$ are [[imp:unusual]]; $z < -3$ or $z > 3$ are [[imp:very unusual]].
About 95% of z‑scores lie between −2 and 2.
Z‑scores are [[imp:unitless]] — they place different variables on a common scale.
They allow comparison of relative standing across different means and standard deviations.
cards.front: Why are z‑scores useful for comparing different data sets?
